source_document: The House of Commons debates a railway between Liverpool and Manchester, 2 March 1825
source_citation: Source: William Huskisson, speech in the House of Commons on the Liverpool and Manchester Rail-Way Bill, 2 March 1825 (adapted). Hansard, HC Deb 2 March 1825, vol. 12, cc. 849-850.
source_text:
It was well known that, under the present system, cotton had been detained [held up] at Liverpool for a fortnight [two weeks], while the manufacturers at Manchester were obliged to suspend their labours: and goods which had been manufactured at Manchester for foreign parts, could not be transmitted to Liverpool in time, on account of the tardy [slow] canal conveyance. Not less than a thousand ton of goods a-day were embarked on these canals between Liverpool and Manchester. . . .
. . . In 1821, only four years ago, the amount of goods exported from the port of Liverpool . . . was 11,500,000l. [pounds] What was the amount in 1824? It was upwards of 19,000,000l.
prompt: Explain the historical circumstances that led to the creation of this document.
intro: No hints, no starter, no checklist. This is the one you do the way you would on the exam. Nobody in this debate explains what was going on - they all already know. That is what you have to work out.
write_it_in: Practice. The one that counts is Make the Case in your casefile - that is your own Historical Context paragraph, and it is scored.
model_response: By the 1820s Manchester's factories were spinning and weaving cotton faster than it could be moved, and Liverpool was the port it went out through. The canals, dug in the century before, were the only way to carry goods in bulk between the two, and Huskisson told Parliament that cotton sat at Liverpool for two weeks while Manchester's mills stood still. Liverpool's exports had gone from 11.5 million pounds in 1821 to more than 19 million in 1824. That gap, between what Britain could now make and what it could actually move, is what led merchants and bankers to ask Parliament for a railway.
